title: BBC Verify: Delhi's Official Diwali Averages Missed Every Reading Above 1,000 Micrograms
excerpt: Comparing CPCB figures with DPCC station data, BBC Verify found 217 missing hourly observations in the Diwali peak window and station averages less than half the DPCC's — while the CPCB blames older analysers capped at 1,000 micrograms.
body:
• BBC Verify found that every hourly PM2.5 reading above 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre recorded by Delhi's DPCC stations on Diwali night was missing from the CPCB's widely cited air quality data.
  • Across the same 30 stations over 24 hours, available CPCB readings averaged 240 micrograms per cubic metre — less than half the 551 average in the DPCC data for the same stations.
  • Between 9 p.m. on November 8 and 7 a.m. on November 9, 217 hourly observations were missing across 59 CPCB stations; only 16 stations reported complete data in the peak window.
  • The CPCB says older analysers calibrated to 1,000 micrograms treat higher values as errors and exclude them — a hardware limit, it says, not under-reporting — and that the older instruments are being replaced.

Delhi's official air quality figures for Diwali night did not capture the full extent of the pollution peak, a BBC Verify analysis has found. Comparing two Indian government datasets, the BBC found significant discrepancies between the readings published by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) — the figures generally cited by Indian media — and the data held by the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), whose stations feed into the CPCB's records. As fireworks lit up Delhi's skies on November 8, every hourly PM2.5 reading above 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre was missing from the CPCB's published data.

We reported the CPCB's initial explanation on November 11 in CPCB Says Diwali Data Gaps Came From Older Monitors' 1,000-Microgram Ceiling. The BBC's station-by-station comparison now puts numbers on how much of the peak went unrecorded.

What the Comparison Shows

Across the same 30 stations over the 24 hours covering Diwali night, available CPCB readings averaged 240 micrograms per cubic metre — less than half the average of 551 in the DPCC's data. Three stations recorded hourly PM2.5 concentrations above 3,000 micrograms in the DPCC data examined by BBC Verify. None of the 116 readings above 1,000 micrograms from the 30 DPCC-managed stations appeared in the CPCB's published records.

The gaps were widest at the peak. Between 21:00 on November 8 and 07:00 on November 9, 217 hourly PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations; only 16 stations reported complete data during that window, while 43 had at least one missing observation. The missing hours matter beyond the headline number: stations need at least 16 hours of valid PM2.5 measurements to calculate a daily average under the CPCB's methodology, so the worst hours dropped out of the daily figures entirely. At RK Puram in south Delhi, where pollution peaked at nearly 2,500 micrograms, BBC Verify calculated an average of about 945 micrograms over the 24 hours after 17:00 on November 8 from the DPCC hourly readings, against 299 micrograms from the CPCB's published data for 14 of those 24 hours. The result: despite the sharp overnight rise, the CPCB reported Delhi's AQI at 344 at 16:00 on November 9, down from 376 at the same time the day before.

Excluding high readings risks misrepresenting actual pollution levels and could cause people to lose trust in official figures.

— Dr Manoj Kumar, Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), to BBC Verify

Dr Sierra Clark, an environmental epidemiologist at City St George's, University of London, warned that classifying high pollution readings as missing could leave out the very days when exposure was most dangerous.

The CPCB's Explanation

The CPCB has said the discrepancies stem from scientific methodology and hardware limitations, not deliberate under-reporting, according to its clarification reported by Tech Word News. Some older particle analysers, deployed when the National Air Quality Index was introduced in 2015, were calibrated to measure up to 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre; the automated system treats values above that range as errors, so those hours are excluded from the station's 24-hour average. The board said older instruments are being replaced and the monitoring network continuously expanded. It also notes that the National AQI reflects exposure over the previous 24 hours rather than a single peak hour, which is why its figures differ from private apps that respond to sharp hourly fluctuations — a distinction the Times of India's own explainer on the Diwali readings also sets out.

For Delhi residents, the practical gap remains: on the year's most polluted night, the official index understated what the city's own monitoring stations recorded. Our earlier coverage of the missing station data is at Delhi Pollution Data Went Missing at Several Stations as Diwali Peak Hit.
